key_insight: Representing imaging data as a quantum state is not enough: input access, measurement, and decoding determine which estimates or decisions are computationally accessible.
engineering_relevance: Quantum imaging workflows require end-to-end resource accounting rather than assuming compact amplitude storage enables efficient full-array readout.
method: Distinguish amplitude-encoded input values from encodings of complete candidate labelings.
Use complementary measurements for unknown-phase inference and matrix SVD to explain pure-state entanglement.
Map a four-pixel segmentation objective to a cost operator and a one-layer QAOA sampling circuit.
evidence_signal: In the four-pixel example, one-layer QAOA lowers mean energy from 1.675 to 0.686 versus uniform sampling, but a nonoptimal labeling is more probable than the optimum (0.484 versus 0.365); archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable boundary decision.
watch_item: Lower mean energy does not guarantee the optimal labeling is the most likely output, and encoding alone does not establish computational advantage.
paper_title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference
